Diego

messages.subject: Re: [simmer-devel] Multiple Cores during simulation
messages.body_plain:
Hi Diego,

Yes, simmer is single-process, as many other DES frameworks: SimPy, SimJulia, OMNET++, Arena (if I'm not mistaken)... This is because there are important reasons for them not to be multi-process, mainly two: 1) the synchronisation problems that a multi-threaded simulation imposes are HUGE, and 2) the performance gains in typical simulation models are uncertain.

But you still may take advantage of your 4 cores. Typically, one simulation alone is insufficient to extract any conclusion. You'll need several runs, several replicas, and that's where you can exploit parallelisation with standard R tools (e.g., the parallel package). Please, take a look at the "Replication" section <http://r-simmer.org/articles/A-introduction.html#replication> of the introductory vignette.

Regards,
Iñaki

messages.subject: Re: [simmer-devel] Using same attribute in more than one trajectory
messages.subject_clean: [simmer-devel] Using same attribute in more than one trajectory
messages.body_plain:
Hi Juan,

What about creating a custom monitor? Take for example the following code:

custom_monitor<-function(){
  results <- data.frame()

  function(time, value){
    if(missing(value)){
      return(results)
    }
    results<<-rbind(results,
                    data.frame(time=time, value=value))
  }
}

You can then create your own (global) monitor:

my_mon<-custom_monitor()
my_mon(5, "firstval")
my_mon(18, "secondval")

Calling my_mon() will return a dataframe with the values:

> my_mon()
  time     value
1    5  firstval
2   18 secondval

This way you could pass the current time, now(env), as the first argument to my_mon() in order to follow the evolution of the variable through time.

Regards,
Bart

messages.subject: Re: Prepare a simulation's initial state
messages.body_plain:
Up to now, when I needed a warmup period I only took this into account in the analysis of the results (and potentially in the runtime).
If w is the warmup time, I simply filtered the monitor's results to exclude everything before w. A nice to have could e.g. be the specification of a warmup time in `run()` which is then taken into account by the `get_mon_` functions.

- B

messages.body_plain:
2016-11-04 17:49 GMT+01:00 Bart Smeets <bartsm...@gmail.com>:
> Up to now, when I needed a warmup period I only took this into account in the analysis of the results (and potentially in the runtime).
> If w is the warmup time, I simply filtered the monitor's results to exclude everything before w. A nice to have could e.g. be the specification of a warmup time in `run()` which is then taken into account by the `get_mon_` functions.

I think simmer should *not* filter data for two reasons:
If the transitory is complex and needs to be determined statistically, you need to do it by yourself in the analysis phase.
If the transitory is straightforward, you can simply filter everything before t=t_0, and that's it: there is no gain in simmer doing so.
It might be some gain if the data saturates your RAM. But if that's the case, the warm-up is probably the smallest of your problems. :D

But turning to the pre-initialisation strategy, there may be systems too dependent on the initial conditions (for instance, reaching very different stationary regimes depending on the initial state), so that you may need to set up these initial conditions maching your particular problem.

I would like to spend time on this issue. At some point... I promise. :D For instance, it would be great if we could identify a simple problem, a specific simulation, exhibiting the behaviour I've described.

--

messages.body_plain:
Hi Diego,

You should call your custom monitor each time you change the value, and always inside a function (otherwise, it’s not dynamically evaluated). For instance:
timeout(function() {
  BlockBin <<- 1
  BlockBin_rec(now(Project), BlockBin)
  return(0)
}) %>%

Iñaki

messages.subject: New vignette: Other SimPy Examples
messages.body_plain:
